messages.subject: Re: [methylkit_discussion] Histogram of % methylation plot
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Your data contains Cs from every possible context. Your plot suggests that 99.8% of Cs are unmethylated (Actually the picture is very small and fonts are difficult to read). So, there are 0.2% Cs that are methylated. To me it seems that the proportion of methylated Cs is too small to be seen on the plot!

If you are working on human genome (not mentioned in your email), consider the fact that genome has very few CpG and among them a higher proportion of them are unmethylated. And a huge majority of Cs in other contexts are also unmethylated (too huge to be compared with methylated Cs in other contexts in terms of numbers). Since your data is dominated by unmethylated Cytosines, it is not surprising to see such a plot! Generally, researchers speak about cytosine methylation in terms of a particular context (not necessary to be followed).

Regards,
Kalyan

Hello,

My name is Claire and I am a current graduate student at the University of Washington.  I am comparing 6 samples using whole-genome bisulfite sequencing using the R package methylKit and have a few questions I'm hoping to get answered.

Any input you can give me would be greatly appreciated and I thank you for your time.
--
Claire E. Olson

messages.subject: Re: [methylkit_discussion] methylkit question
messages.body_plain:
Just to clarify- are you doing an n-of-1 study, with the data drawn at different time points? If so, I would suggest you run the analysis multiple times, with a different time point as the 'case' (treatment=1) each time (you can use the reorganize fuction in methylKit to change your treatment vector to do this). This will allow you to identify methylation differences that are characteristic for each time point. See how that compares to similar array-based studies as appropriate for your tissue and species: see this paper <http://genomebiology.com/2013/14/10/r115> and some of its references.

Two different tests are used depending on the number of samples: if you're comparing 1 vs 1, Fisher's exact test <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher's_exact_test> is used. Otherwise, logistic regression <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logistic_regression> (also known as a binomial GLM <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_linear_model> with a logit link) is used to compare the means of the two groups. In either case, coverage is taken into account. If you're using the get.methylDiff function, it's filtering for sites with qvalues<.01 and methylation differences of >25%. Depending on your data, this may be too stringent- you have a relatively low number of sites, so I'd consider raising the qvalue threshold.

Dhruva

messages.body_plain:
differential methylation by definition requires a control group. If you are interested in comparing two stages of development it is OK to assume one of them is the control just remember which one is which when you do the interpretation.

 But, I guess what you are interested is specific methylation patterns that change over the course of the development (more than 2 timepoints ?). You can do multiple things to make headway on this. In addition, in methylKit, DMRs are the regions of the genome that are predefined, such as equi-width tiles over the genome, or promoter regions. So I assume that you tiled your data since you want to get DMRs (regions).

You can read-in all your samples at once keeping the order of the developmental stages, do the tiling and then do unite(). then get the methylation matrix using percMethylation() then do clustering on the rows of the matrix as Dhruva suggested and make a heatmap. But this will take a lot of time if you are using whole-genome data. Alternative is to use PCA on the matrix of methylation values. This could get you some patterns that explain the variation of your data, and those patterns may correspond to actual changes in methylation that are shared by multiple DMRs.

Another alternative is to calculate the variation of the rows of the methylation matrix, and get the ones that have high variation and do clustering or PCA on them to see the shared patterns among regions of varying methylation.

Here is discussion about coverage in differential methylation calculation
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/methylkit_discussion/Li$20/methylkit_discussion/_6LlMiPH_98/xZVsXbl-sMgJ

Filtering the bases before performing 'unite' may not give desired results in this case.

Read every CpG (no coverage cutoff)
Remove CpG with extremely high coverage using 'normalizeCoverage'
Perform 'unite' (destrand=T)
Filter CpGs with a given threshold across all the samples
